paragraphs: Aircraft structure, surfaces, rigging, and systems assemblers (U.S. counterpart: O*NET/BLS 51-2011 Aircraft Structure, Surfaces, Rigging, and Systems Assemblers) assemble, fit, fasten, and install components of aircraft, spacecraft, or missiles in aircraft manufacturing and final assembly: they determine assembly sequence and part relationships according to drawings, process documents, and specifications; position and align parts on fixtures and tooling; rivet, bond, and fasten structural members; install and adjust flight-control, control, rigging, and environmental control systems; measure and inspect assembly dimensions and fits; fabricate and fit the required parts; and record assembly and inspection results. The workplace is the assembly shop and the final assembly line; the core metrics are assembly precision, structural integrity, and record traceability, not aircraft maintenance release or operation. People for whom it may be worth exploring this path are usually willing to work step by step according to drawings and processes, can maintain manual precision and dimensional sensitivity over long periods, and are prepared for responsibility for assembly quality.

First do the D-v1 paper exercise on this page: check four simulated records against three explicitly given dimensional ranges, then handle the D-v2 supplement form. Deliver two versions of the checklist, the anomalies, and the supplementary-evidence list; the reference answers, the ten-point self-check, and the seven-day steps are all in the pathway section. It is used to experience tolerance checking, version awareness, and record discipline; it is not an on-site skills test or a recruitment test.

People more likely to adapt: those who can work step by step according to drawings and process documents without skipping steps, are willing to use calipers, plug gauges, and measuring instruments to repeatedly verify dimensions and tolerances, can maintain manual precision and stamina over long periods while wearing protective equipment as required, and hold a sense of reverence for structural integrity and responsibility for assembly quality. If someone is unwilling to execute according to the process, tends to skip measurements or records based on experience, or is uncomfortable with the coordination and escalation in the final-assembly rhythm, the risk is usually greater.

In one sentence: a manufacturing position that assembles, fits, fastens, and installs aircraft structural components and flight-control, control, and environmental control systems in assembly shops and on final assembly lines according to drawings and processes, completing measurement, inspection, and recordkeeping.

The tasks of aircraft structure, surfaces, rigging, and systems assemblers fall into four categories: drawing reading and process preparation (reading drawings, diagrams, or specifications to determine layout, work sequence, and part relationships, and marking identification information on tubing or cable assemblies); part and tooling preparation (preparing parts, standard components, and tooling according to the process; cutting, trimming, filing, bending, or grinding parts to ensure fit and clearance; and setting up and operating pipe-bending, cutting, forming, and other equipment according to specifications); positioning and assembly (positioning and aligning parts with fixtures, tooling, and measuring instruments; assembling parts and subassemblies; riveting, bonding, or welding to secure brackets and connectors; installing skins and structural members; and joining structural assemblies such as wings, tail assemblies, and fuselages); and systems installation and inspection (installing and checking control cables and actuators with tension meters; aligning and adjusting rigging and control systems to the specified tolerances; installing mechanical linkages and actuators; inspecting and testing the fit, alignment, performance, and compliance of assemblies; and cleaning up and recycling work waste while recording results).

O*NET 51-2011.00 Aircraft Structure, Surfaces, Rigging, and Systems Assemblers: assemble, fit, fasten, and install parts of aircraft, spacecraft, or missiles, such as tail assemblies, wings, fuselages, bulkheads, stabilizers, landing gear, rigging and control equipment, or heating and ventilation systems. Common job titles include Aircraft Assembler, Aircraft Line Assembler, Assembler, Assembly Riveter, Assembly Technician, sheet-metal assembler and riveter (SMAR), sheet-metal mechanic, sheet-metal technician, structural mechanic, and structural technician.

values: Paper exercise D-v1: a fictional display frame, not an aircraft and not a physical operation. All units are mm; judge only according to the given rules, and do not purchase measuring instruments. The valid drawing version is V2; the old V1 is obsolete. V2: length L=100.00±0.10; hole distance P=40.00, with permitted deviation -0.05/+0.15; fit clearance G≤0.20 and G≥0. Boundary values are included in the permitted range.

Record A: drawing version V2, measuring-instrument status valid; L=100.10, P=39.95, G=0.20. Record B: drawing version V2, measuring-instrument status valid; L=99.88, P=40.16, G=0.18. Record C: drawing version V1, measuring-instrument status valid; L=100.00, P=40.00, G=0.10. Record D: drawing version V2, measuring-instrument status expired; L=100.00, P=40.00, G=0.10. All inputs are simulated values.

Problem rules: first check the drawing version and measuring-instrument status. Give a numerical judgment only when both are valid; otherwise mark the entire record 'pending supplementary evidence' and do not mark it as conforming. If any valid dimension is out of bounds, mark the entire record 'does not conform to the problem statement'; do not treat a retest or verbal approval as eliminating the original record.

Supplement D-v2: B's new valid retest values are L=100.02, P=40.10, G=0.18, with drawing version V2; C has been re-measured with V2 and a valid measuring instrument to obtain L=100.00, P=40.00, G=0.10; D has no supplementary record. Preserve the D-v1 original values, write the D-v2 conclusions separately, and do not overwrite the old records.

Deliver a four-row checklist: record number, version, measuring-instrument status, the three permitted ranges, measured values, item-by-item judgments, the overall conclusion, and its basis. Also list the derivation of the valid ranges; P's tolerance must not be mistaken for ±0.15.

Write one anomaly record for B: state the original value and which boundary it exceeds, suspend use of that conclusion, and hand it to the record reviewer designated in the problem statement for verification; there is no physical rework task. For C and D, list the missing valid evidence separately.

Then form the D-v2 four-row conclusions and change notes according to the supplement, noting that B is a newly added retest, C is a newly added valid record, and D remains pending supplementary evidence. Finally, self-check row by row against the reference results.

Reference ranges: L is [99.90,100.10]; P is [39.95,40.15]; G is [0,0.20]. D-v1: A's three items are all within bounds and conform to the problem statement; B's L is 0.02 below the lower bound, P is 0.01 above the upper bound, and G is within bounds, so the entire record does not conform to the problem statement.

Although C's values are within range, it uses the obsolete V1, so the entire record is pending supplementary evidence; although D's values are within range, the measuring-instrument status is expired, so the entire record is pending supplementary evidence. subject.summary: Aircraft structure, surfaces, rigging, and systems assemblers assemble, fit, fasten, and install structural components of aircraft, spacecraft, or missiles and their flight-control, control, rigging, and environmental control systems in assembly shops and on final assembly lines, following drawings and process specifications, and complete measurement, inspection, and recordkeeping; the key points for judgment are reading drawings and understanding tolerances, special-process qualifications and process authorization, and responsibility for assembly quality.
